paras: The lynching of Eli Bryant was the hanging of a Black man by a white mob at Harges Station, near Starkville, Mississippi, on July 27, 1888. Bryant had been accused of assaulting a white woman, and papers reported that a crowd of 500 to 800 men hanged him after he was caught. The story went out by wire and ran in Southern, Northern and Mississippi papers over the next three weeks, usually presenting his guilt as settled.

According to a special dispatch from Starkville to the Memphis Appeal, Bryant was accused of having raped a white woman the previous Saturday near the line between Oktibbeha and Winston counties. A wire report from Aberdeen called the charge an "indecent assault" on a "respectable white lady," while two Mississippi papers described her as a "married lady." The woman was not named, and she was reported to be in very critical condition but expected to recover.

Bryant was caught near Sturgis on the night of July 26, and the Aberdeen report said great excitement prevailed all day at Harges' station over his arrest. The wire said the woman identified him and that he "admitted the deed." The Memphis Appeal reported that a mob of "between 500 and 800 well-to-do white citizens" hanged him at about 2 o'clock on July 27.

In the Appeal's account, Bryant confessed "in a free manner," offered no resistance, and asked the crowd to hurry because he was "going to glory." These details came only from the reporters' and the crowd's side, and no other version of his last words appears in the coverage.
No report of an inquest, arrests or grand jury action appears in the coverage, and no member of the mob was named.

The Memphis Appeal ran its dispatch on July 28 under the headline "Eli Bryant Hanged" with the deck "The Negro Rapist Strung by a Mob," treating the accusation as fact. The Aberdeen wire, relayed through New Orleans, appeared the same day in the Savannah Morning News as "Hanged by a Mob" and three days later in the Atlanta Constitution as "Justice Meted Out." In both versions the hanging shared a dispatch with a separate killing at Eden, Mississippi.

Northern dailies printed shorter forms of the wire, the Daily Kennebec Journal under "'Vigilance' Law" and the Burlington Weekly Free Press under "A Tale of Crime in Mississippi." Midwestern weekly digests reduced the story to one line, several of them placing Starkville in Louisiana. Within Mississippi, the Brookhaven Leader and the Liberty Southern Herald gave the case one sentence each in their state columns, spelling the name "Bryan" and placing it in Winston County.

A digest item that circulated in Northern weeklies from August 9 said "Eli Bryan" was lynched "on the 4th" in "Winslow County," Mississippi. Because the same-day dispatches from Starkville and Aberdeen give July 27, and the River Falls Journal had printed the July 27 version a week earlier, the later item is best read as a misdating of the same hanging.

reader.title: Lynching of Eli Bryant
bases: A Memphis Appeal special and an Aberdeen wire both report that a mob hanged Eli Bryant, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, at Harges Station near Starkville, Miss. (A1, A4, A6).

Bryant was hanged by a mob, put at 500 to 800 men in the Memphis Appeal, with no legal proceeding reported, over an accusation of assault on a white woman (A1, A4). The headline 'Justice Meted Out' and the Appeal's account of the hanging as justice show the pretext of justice (A1, A6).
A special dispatch from Starkville to the Memphis Appeal (A1) and a separate Aberdeen wire (A2, A4) agree on the core event, and two Mississippi papers repeat it (A13, A19).

accounts.label: Starkville special dispatch (Memphis Appeal)
accounts.gist: Bryant, accused of raping a white lady the previous Saturday near the Oktibbeha-Winston line, was caught near Sturgis the night before and hanged about 2 o'clock by 500 to 800 'well-to-do white citizens'; he was said to have confessed, offered no resistance and asked them to hurry.

accounts.label: Aberdeen wire (via New Orleans)
accounts.gist: At Harges' station near Starkville there was great excitement all day over Bryant's arrest for an indecent assault on a respectable white lady; a mob hanged him after the woman identified him and he 'admitted the deed'.

accounts.label: Mississippi state columns
accounts.gist: Eli Bryan was hanged in Winston county for criminal assault upon a married lady, having been identified and having confessed.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headlined 'The Negro Rapist Strung by a Mob' and stressed his confession and wish that the mob 'mete justice out to him'; the Atlanta Constitution ran the wire as 'Justice Meted Out'.
Northern papers carried the Aberdeen wire beside the Eden killings under headlines like '"Vigilance" Law' and 'A Tale of Crime in Mississippi', or as one line in weekly digests.

conflicts.note: The July 27 date comes from same-day dispatches from Starkville and Aberdeen; the 'on the 4th' item appeared in digests nearly two weeks later and is the weaker evidence. The same River Falls Journal ran the July 27 version a week before (A11).
Mississippi is given by the datelined dispatches and by Mississippi papers; the 'La.' is a digest error.
Only the Memphis Appeal gives an hour; nothing in the coverage supports 4 o'clock.

Harges Station, near Starkville, Miss.; the alleged assault took place near the Oktibbeha-Winston county line, and Bryant was caught near Sturgis
Eli Bryant (also printed 'Ell Bryant', 'En Bryant', 'Eli Bryan'), described as a negro or 'colored'

Accused of an 'indecent assault' on a 'respectable white lady' (Aberdeen wire), of having 'raped a white lady last Saturday' (Memphis Appeal), or of 'criminal assault upon a married lady' (Mississippi papers)

Papers reported that the woman was in very critical condition but might recover
